title: ROLAND: Graph Learning Framework for Dynamic Graphs

problem.claim: Existing dynamic graph neural network approaches do not adequately address model design, evaluation settings, and scalable training for evolving graphs.

gap.claim: Dynamic GNNs do not incorporate state-of-the-art static GNN designs, current evaluations do not fully reflect graph evolution, and common training methods are not scalable.

contributions.claim: ROLAND is a graph representation learning framework that enables static GNNs to be repurposed for dynamic graphs by recurrently updating hierarchical node states over time.
ROLAND introduces a live-update evaluation setting that simulates rolling prediction and model updates for dynamic graphs.
ROLAND provides a scalable and efficient dynamic-GNN training approach based on incremental training and meta-learning.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments cover eight dynamic graph datasets on future link prediction tasks.
Under standard evaluation settings on three datasets, ROLAND models achieve an average 62.7% relative MRR improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.

ROLAND scales to dynamic graphs with 56 million edges, while the reported baselines experience out-of-memory errors on larger datasets; after re-implementation with the ROLAND training strategy, ROLAND models retain an average 15.5% relative MRR improvement.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNNs have been successfully applied to many real-world static graphs.
This success has not transferred fully to dynamic graphs because of limitations in model design, evaluation, and training scalability.
ROLAND repurposes static GNNs for dynamic graphs by treating layer-wise node embeddings as hierarchical states and updating them recurrently over time.
The framework adds live-update evaluation and scalable incremental-training and meta-learning procedures.
Experiments on eight datasets report improvements over baselines and scalability to graphs with 56 million edges.

source_observation.claim: Layer-wise node embeddings are treated as hierarchical node states and recurrently updated over time.

interpretation.claim: Representing static-model internals as evolving states can provide a reuse path from static to dynamic learning.

application.claim: When adapting static graph models to temporal settings, preserve multi-layer representations as state variables and update them incrementally.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this strategy generalizes beyond the reported dynamic graph tasks and datasets.

source_observation.claim: The authors introduce live-update evaluation and report scalability benefits from incremental training and meta-learning.

interpretation.claim: Evaluation and training procedures should model deployment-time graph evolution and resource constraints.

application.claim: For evolving-graph systems, evaluate rolling prediction-and-update cycles and use incremental training where full retraining is not scalable.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the computational costs, operational constraints, or failure cases of the proposed procedures.

unknowns: The eight datasets and their characteristics are not identified.
The static GNN architectures, hierarchical-state design details, and update equations are not specified.
The live-update protocol and baseline implementation details are not provided.
Statistical variation, confidence intervals, and per-dataset results are not reported.
